note: Web research against Polish Wikipedia + zabytek.pl + the Łódź regional heritage catalogue. Caveats below are load-bearing — two entries are NOT what the batch framing assumed, and one name is a typology rather than a building.
caveats: ⛔ 'Kamienica Wielkomiejska' IS NOT A UNIQUE BUILDING NAME. *Kamienica wielkomiejska* ('grand metropolitan tenement') is a Łódź building TYPOLOGY — dozens exist (Piotrkowska 12, 90, 101, 215; Jaracza 37; etc.). Resolved to the one indexed under that bare name at Sienkiewicza 52 (1913, Leon Doński), CONFIDENCE LOW. If the OSM tag meant a specific address, re-resolve from the building_id before authoring.
⭐ TWO DISTINCT GROHMAN VILLAS, routinely conflated on the web: HENRYK's at Tymienieckiego 24, LUDWIK's at Tylna 9/11. Separate buildings, separate articles. Do not merge.

Milsz/Milsch name conflict: zabytek.pl and the regional catalogue say 'willa Hermana Juliusza Milsza'; Polish Wikipedia titles the SAME building (Łąkowa 21 / Kopernika 46) 'Willa Teodora Milscha'. Disputed given name, same structure. A separate street is also named after Milsch — don't conflate.

⚠️ ARCHITECT ATTRIBUTION IS FLAGGED, NOT ASSERTED. For Henryk Grohman's villa and the Goldfeder palace, Polish Wikipedia states that Hilary Majewski's signature on the plans 'does not settle authorship' — as city architect he signed off drawings he did not necessarily draw. Preserved rather than flattened.

⚠️ FRAMING ERROR (mine): I briefed these as 'industrialist palaces/villas of the textile barons'. Collegium Anatomicum was built as a CHARITABLE OLD-AGE SHELTER; Goldfeder was a BANKER, not a manufacturer; Gehlig was a BUILDER/CONTRACTOR. Decide whether the guide absorbs or drops them — do not let the framing rewrite what they are.
Geyer's dworek has no recorded architect in any source found — left null rather than guessed.

entries.name: Dworek Ludwika Geyera
entries.blurb: 1833 house of Ludwik Geyer, who opened Łódź's first steam-powered cotton mill. One of the oldest surviving buildings in the city; the 1948 remont added the columned porch.
entries.why_notable: Oldest surviving industrialist residence in Łódź; part of the Geyer factory complex declared a Pomnik Historii in 2015.

entries.name: Pałac Karola Poznańskiego
entries.style: Eclectic / neo-Renaissance with Art Nouveau detail
entries.blurb: Palace built 1904–08 for Karol Poznański, son of cotton magnate Izrael Poznański, with a facade modelled on Florentine palazzi. Home of the Łódź Academy of Music since 1945.
entries.why_notable: Zeligson's Florentine-palazzo facade; seat of the Grażyna and Kiejstut Bacewicz Academy of Music.

entries.name: Willa Henryka Grohmana
entries.architect: Hilary Majewski (attributed — plans signed by him; authorship unsettled)
entries.style: Italian neo-Renaissance exterior; Viennese Secession interiors
entries.blurb: Villa at Tymienieckiego 24, built 1892–93 for Henryk Grohman and remodelled 1903 and 1912. Its Secession interiors house the Museum of Artistic Books since 1993.
entries.why_notable: Rare intact Viennese-Secession interior in Łódź; now the Muzeum Książki Artystycznej.

entries.name: Willa Hermana Juliusza Milsza
entries.blurb: Neo-Renaissance villa at Łąkowa 21 / Kopernika 46, built 1870–82 beside the Milsch brewery. Rusticated facade, Ionic half-columns and a three-storey spired tower.
entries.why_notable: Brewer's villa with a tower dominant; later the Łódź butchers' guild house, now a pub and cultural venue.

entries.name: Dom Hilarego Majewskiego
entries.blurb: House at Włókiennicza 11 that Łódź's city architect Hilary Majewski built for himself, 1883–86. Later split into flats; restored 2023, revealing original painted decoration.
entries.why_notable: Self-designed home of the architect responsible for much of 19th-century Łódź.

entries.name: Dom Otto Gehliga
entries.style: German Renaissance Revival with Dutch Mannerist detail
entries.blurb: Tuwima 17: a weaver's house that builder Otto Gehlig rebuilt for himself in 1883, adding flanking pavilions and a steep decorated roof. Pompeian-style ceiling polychromy survives inside.
entries.why_notable: Rare Łódź example of German Renaissance / Dutch Mannerist ornament; listed only in 2006.

entries.name: Collegium Anatomicum
entries.blurb: Narutowicza 60, built 1894–96 as the shelter for the elderly and disabled of the Łódź Christian Charity Society. Became a Medical University anatomy building after 1945.
entries.why_notable: Large charitable institution building by city architect Chełmiński, erected by Otto Gehlig's firm.

entries.name: Kamienica Wielkomiejska
entries.blurb: Monumental tenement at Sienkiewicza 52, built 1913 to Leon Doński's design — one of the last large Łódź apartment blocks raised before the First World War.
entries.why_notable: Late, monumental example of the Łódź grand-tenement type, built on the eve of WWI.

entries.name: Willa Ludwika Grohmana
entries.blurb: Villa at Tylna 9/11 built 1881–94 for textile manufacturer Ludwik Grohman. Its former garden is now Kiliński Park; listed in the heritage register (A/99) in 1971.
entries.why_notable: Grohman family seat by city architect Majewski; its grounds became a public park.

entries.name: Pałac Maksymiliana Goldfedera
entries.architect: Bronisław Żochowski (plans signed by Hilary Majewski, likely co-author)
entries.blurb: Piotrkowska 77, built 1891–92 for banker Maksymilian Goldfeder as combined residence and banking house. Single-storey, with a facade modelled on 16th-century Florentine and Roman palaces.
entries.why_notable: Banker's, not manufacturer's, palace on Piotrkowska; recently restored.
